claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature metastable BCC phase.
Non-uniform cooling with thermal gradients or mechanical constraint generates significant residual stress.
Cooling-induced residual stress increases the local dislocation density.
Dislocation networks provide fast diffusion pathways in the BCC matrix.
Dislocations act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for secondary phases.
Residual-stress-enhanced diffusion promotes local elemental partitioning in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The proposed partitioning particularly involves Co and Al.
Stress and dislocation structures are coupled to atomic segregation at grain boundaries and within grains.
Local elemental partitioning reduces the local interfacial free energy.
Residual-stress-assisted partitioning lowers the nucleation barrier for secondary-phase formation.
The proposed mechanism enables nucleation and growth of ordered B2 or FCC regions.
After identical isothermal exposure, non-uniformly cooled samples will contain more localized secondary phases than stress-relieved controls.
Secondary phases and compositional gradients will be localized preferentially in regions of high dislocation density.
Measured residual stress will correlate spatially with enhanced phase transformation.
Slow, uniform, stress-relieved cooling followed by isothermal exposure will retain a predominantly near-homogeneous BCC microstructure.
The mechanism requires both significant residual stress and sufficient temperature and time for diffusion-driven partitioning.
Cooling that is too rapid suppresses formation of the proposed enhanced diffusion pathways and therefore suppresses secondary-phase nucleation.
Cooling sufficiently slowly to permit complete stress relaxation suppresses the proposed enhanced diffusion pathways and secondary-phase nucleation.
Annealing at 600–650 °C permits diffusion and potential phase nucleation in the investigated alloy.
A qualitative causal link between residual-stress-enhanced diffusion and phase nucleation is established sufficiently to be described as sound.
